newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Kinkel welcomes return of lira to ERM.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Kinkel welcomes return of lira to ERM.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel on Monday welcomed the return of the Italian lira to the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM), the currency grid which is a precursor to the launch of a common European currency.
"With its participation in the Exchange Rate Mechanism, Italy is committing itself to continuing its courageous and determined savings and stability policies," Kinkel said.
"Italy will thereby strengthen the credibility of its convergence policies on the financial markets," he added in a statement.

Italy, booted out of the ERM in 1992 by a wall of foreign exchange bets against the lira, will rejoin the grid -- which has 15 percent fluctuation bands -- with a central rate of 990 lira to the mark, European partners agreed at the weekend.

But officials from the so-called hard currency core of Europe, led by Germany, made it clear in Brussels that returning to the European currency club did not mean Italy would be sure to join the planned launch of the euro in 1999.

Kinkel said the line-up for monetary union would be determined in early 1998 based on a tight interpretation of the Maastricht treaty. Under Maastricht, countries must conform to several criteria, and most -- including Italy -- are struggling to cut back public debt and budget deficits.

"At the beginning of 1998 we will take a decision on the group of participants in the light of how the convergence criteria are achieved by then. There will be no weakening of the Maastricht criteria," Kinkel said.
"All member countries are called on to make determined efforts to fulfil the convergence criteria and qualify for entry."
